project.name: TabMates
project.description: Kotlin Multiplatform + Compose Multiplatform app for splitting shared expenses across groups, settling up across Android, iOS, Desktop and Web from a single shared codebase. Clean Architecture + MVI, offline-first with Room.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to understand what TabMates is: a Kotlin Multiplatform + Compose Multiplatform app that splits shared expenses across groups, running on Android, iOS, Desktop, and Web. It frames the feature set you'll explore (Groups, multi-currency Expenses, offline-first sync, Settle up, Activity feed, Accounts, push notifications) and the tech stack (Clean Architecture, MVI, Koin, Navigation 3, Ktor, Room). The architecture.html doc complements it with a visual map of the layered, feature-modularized structure that the rest of this tour walks through in code.

tour.title: Shared App Shell
tour.description: App.kt is the common entry point shared by every platform: it composes the theme, sets up navigation, and wires the sync coordinators that keep data fresh. This single composable is the trunk from which the entire dependency graph grows, so understanding what it pulls together gives you a bird's-eye view of the runtime. The sibling sync coordinators (Currency/Group/Notifications) and DeepLinkHandler hint at the offline-first and invite-link features described in the README.
tour.languageLesson: In Compose Multiplatform, a single @Composable in commonMain becomes the shared UI for all targets. Platform-specific behavior is injected via 'expect/actual' declarations and Koin modules rather than duplicating the screen per platform.

tour.title: Dependency Injection Wiring
tour.description: AppModule is where the :app module assembles every feature and core Koin module into a single dependency graph that App.kt boots. This is the seam that connects the otherwise-isolated feature modules, so reading it reveals which subsystems exist and how they plug together. It embodies the README's modular Clean Architecture: each layer ships its own module, and the app shell is the only place that knows about all of them.
tour.languageLesson: Koin uses a DSL where modules declare 'single', 'factory', and 'viewModel' bindings. Composing modules (rather than one giant graph) keeps each feature self-contained and independently testable.

tour.title: Core Domain: Result & Errors
tour.description: These three types are the most depended-upon nodes in the whole codebase (DataError, Result, and UiText top the fan-in ranking). Result<T, E> is a typed success/failure wrapper, DataError enumerates the failure modes, and UiText bridges domain errors to localized UI strings. Every repository, ViewModel, and validation path speaks this vocabulary, so internalizing it now makes every later step easier to read.
tour.languageLesson: Kotlin's sealed interfaces let Result<T, E> model success and failure as exhaustive 'when' branches with no exceptions. Extension functions like map/onSuccess/onFailure give a fluent, railway-oriented style for chaining fallible operations.

tour.title: Core Data: Networking & Secure Storage
tour.description: The core data layer provides the cross-cutting plumbing every feature reuses. HttpClientExt configures the shared Ktor HttpClient (serialization, logging, auth headers), while SecureStore and KSafeSessionStorage persist tokens securely and back the SessionStorage domain contract from Step 4's domain layer. This is the offline-first/auth foundation: tokens stored here authorize the network calls that feature repositories make.

tour.title: Authentication Feature
tour.description: Authentication is the first vertical feature, structured in the Clean Architecture slices the README promises. AuthService is the domain contract; KtorAuthService implements it against the backend using the core Ktor client and session storage from Step 5; LoginViewModel drives the MVI login screen. This is the canonical example of the domain → data → presentation flow you'll see repeated in every feature.
tour.languageLesson: The MVI pattern here splits each screen into immutable State, an Action sealed type for user intents, and one-shot Event for navigation/toasts. The ViewModel reduces Actions into new State and emits Events, keeping the composable a pure render of State.

tour.title: TabGroup Domain: Groups & Models
tour.description: The tabgroup feature is the heart of the app. Its domain layer defines the data model: Group and GroupParticipant describe a shared group, while TabEntry (the second-highest fan-in node) models an expense entry. GroupRepository is the domain contract for the full group lifecycle, including create/invite/join-via-link from the README. These models are the shared language for every screen and data source that follows.

tour.title: Expenses & Multi-Currency Splitting
tour.description: Building on the TabEntry model from Step 7, this step covers how expenses get split. SplitType encodes the splitting strategy (equal, exact, percentage), Currency and the exchange-rate machinery enable the README's multi-currency support, and the AddExpense screen is the MVI surface where users record a shared cost. Together they turn a raw amount into per-participant shares across currencies.

tour.title: Offline-First & The Room Outbox
tour.description: This is the README's offline-first promise made concrete. OfflineFirstTabEntryRepository serves data from the Room cache and falls back to the network, TabEntryOutbox durably queues writes (backed by PendingOutboxEntity) so actions taken offline survive process death, and TabEntryRealtimeSync applies incoming WebSocket updates. The result: the UI reads instantly from local Room data while writes are reconciled with the server when connectivity returns.
tour.languageLesson: Room on KMP generates type-safe DAOs from @Entity/@Dao annotations. The outbox pattern decouples user intent from network delivery: writes commit locally first, then a coordinator drains the queue, giving optimistic UI and durable offline edits.

tour.title: Settle Up: Balances & Debt Simplification
tour.description: Once expenses are split, TabMates computes who owes whom. PerPersonBalanceCalculator derives each participant's net balance from the entries in Step 8, and DebtSimplifier minimizes the number of transfers needed to settle the group (the README's debt simplification). The SettleUpViewModel presents these suggested payments through the same MVI pattern, closing the loop from 'record an expense' to 'pay each other back'.

tour.title: Push Notifications
tour.description: The notifications feature keeps users informed of group activity. PushNotificationController is the platform-agnostic domain contract, while MobilePushNotificationController (FCM/Firebase on Android & iOS) and WebPushNotificationController (Firebase JS) are the per-platform actual implementations. NotificationDeepLinkBus connects a tapped notification back to the in-app navigation set up by the App shell in Step 2.
tour.languageLesson: KMP's 'expect/actual' mechanism lets PushNotificationController be one common interface with distinct platform actuals: FCM on mobile, Firebase JS on web, a no-op on desktop. Common code depends only on the expectation, never the concrete SDK.

tour.title: Platform Entry Points
tour.description: Each target has a thin launcher that hosts the shared App.kt from Step 2. MainActivity.kt bootstraps Android, the desktop and web main.kt files start the JVM and Wasm/JS builds, and iOSApp.swift hosts the Compose UI inside a SwiftUI app. They prove the README's promise: one shared codebase, four native shells, with platform wiring isolated to these files.

tour.title: CI Pipeline & Contributor Guide
tour.description: Finally, the capstone: how code stays healthy. The GitHub Actions pr_pipeline runs formatting checks and builds/tests the Android target on every pull request, while AGENTS.md documents the conventions (module layout, MVI, Koin, testing) that keep this multi-module codebase consistent. Together they encode the project's quality bar and onboarding contract for new contributors.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows use 'on' triggers to run 'jobs' of sequential 'steps'. Caching the Gradle dependencies between runs is what keeps KMP CI builds (which compile for multiple targets) from timing out.
